# Colony History
[italic]A short history of Gixen's Caverns for new arrivals, as the Herald's archive tells it.[/italic]
## The Surface Above us is desert: rock, dust, cactus and the odd Joshua tree, with nothing worth building on. The survey crews wanted what was underneath.
## Going Down The rock is honeycombed with natural caverns, and the seams the surveyors were after run straight through them. Digging a colony into the caves was cheaper than sealing one against the surface, and it kept the dust and the heat off the workers. So the settlement went down. Offices, bunks, workshops and mess halls were cut into the cavern walls one level at a time, and the mining crews kept going deeper. Some of the deepest galleries opened onto chambers of cut sandstone that no colony crew ever dug. The Administration calls them a geological curiosity and keeps the doors shut.
## The Tunnels - A transit line run by the colony's Department of Transportation links the levels, the pits and the powerstation. The platform is the closest thing we have to a town square. - Power comes from the thermal generators at the powerstation, which draw on the heat of the deep rock. When they stop, so do the lights, the pumps and the trains. - The landing zone sits up on the mountain. Every crate, every new arrival and every body sent home goes up and down that one route.
## The Air The caverns hold pockets of gas that nobody mapped, and when a dig breaks into one the oxygen can drop in seconds. That is why the warning signs are posted on the walls and every work area keeps an emergency oxygen kit. Children here learn where the nearest kit is before they can read the signs.
## The People Gixen's Caverns is a United Americas colony of miners, engineers, transit crews and the people who feed and patch them. Residents are proud of the place and blunt about it: it is dark, it is cramped, and it is home. Not all of them are content with the arrangement, and slogans against the UA turn up on the tunnel walls faster than the D.O.T. can paint over them.
## The Press The Herald keeps the archive: who was hurt on which level, which kits were empty and which warnings went unread. We write it down so the next shift knows.
